newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: Mauritius bourse slumps, awaits cabinet reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Mauritius bourse slumps, awaits cabinet reshuffle.

text.p: Only a long-awaited cabinet reshuffle, expected to give a new direction to government, can end the lack of investor confidence which has depressed the Mauritius stock exchange, analysts said.
They told Reuters on Thursday that a key feature of the reshuffle would be the post of finance minister, vacant since Rundhheersing Bheenick resigned on August 6.
Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam temporarily holds the job.

"The sooner Ramgoolam names a new finance minister, the better it will be," Stock Exchange of Mauritius (SEM) Chairman Bruno Hardy said in an interview. "If the competence of the new finance minister is established, this will give back confidence to investment in the stock exchange."
The market Semdex index is hovering just above the psychologically-important support level of 300 and closed at 305.41 on Wednesday -- a new low for the year.
The index was last seen around that range in December 1993 amid a bull run which propelled it to an all-time high of 484 points in January 1995.

The bourse is now capitalised at 28.8 billion rupees ($1.4 billion) with 42 listed companies compared to as much as 29.2 billion rupees ($1.6 billion at then current exchange rates) in January 1995 when there were just 36 listed companies.

Semdex started 1996 at 344.44 but slumped to 315.49 a few days after Bheenick presented a controversial and heavily criticised 1996/97 budget which sought to raise sales tax as well as taxes on productive sectors of the economy.
"The budget was an exercise which was badly received by the population and is the single largest factor that broke investor confidence," Hardy said, explaining where the problem began.
After the government amended the budget to appease critics Semdex remained in a tight 320-325 range until late September when it broke a 320-point floor to slip to its present level.

"Between July and September, there was no big trading volume as investors were not ready to sell below a certain level," Hardy said. "After that, reports from the Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), (and) Africa Emerging Markets Funds rekindled the confidence crisis."

A recently issued EIU country report on Mauritius painted a subdued picture of the island's future economic prospects with growth forecast at 4.0 percent in 1997 from 6.0 percent in 1996 and blamed Ramgoolam's government for losing opportunities.
The Africa Emerging Markets Funds magazine said Mauritius was now the worst performing bourse in Africa.
Leading listed companies released good profit growth figures in September but, overshadowed by scepticism on the political scene, failed to fuel a stock rally, bourse officials said.

Government economic forecasts point towards a good 1996, with gross domestic product (GDP) growth estimated at 6.0 percent and the pillars of the economy, sugar and textiles exports and tourism poised to achieve record earnings.

"Although the (political) climate is not ideal, I am a buyer on the market. Stock prices in some sectors such as hotels, certain sugars, banks and insurance, are cheap in this grossly undervalued market," said Didier Merven of investment advisory and management firm Actuarial & Capital Management Services.
Merven saw shares as attractive because dividend yields were higher than the 8.0 percent savings rate in banks. Market price earnings ratios would sink below 10 as prices fell, he added.
"The government must do something precise. We haven't heard of an economic vision for the next five years," Merven said.
($1=20.565 Mauritian rupees)
